summary: Adds new IPFIX Information Elements so flow records can carry BGP community information, including standard communities (RFC 1997), extended communities (RFC 4360), and large communities (RFC 8092). Operators can then group traffic statistics by their BGP community plans. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: Network traffic reports normally count packets by who sent them. This adds labels from the routing system so the counts can be grouped by those labels instead.

questions: how to export bgp communities in ipfix
what are ipfix element ids 483 to 491
subtitle: New IPFIX fields let routers report which BGP communities a traffic flow belongs to, so traffic can be counted per customer group or region.

tldr.problem: Flow reports by IP address are too fine for a large backbone and reports by AS number are too coarse, and IPFIX had no way to carry BGP community tags that operators use to mark customers, services and regions.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines nine new IPFIX Information Elements: one for each community type (standard, extended, large) plus source and destination lists built as basicLists, so an Exporter can attach the communities of a flow's source and destination addresses to its flow record.
tldr.outcome: Collectors, SDN controllers and PCEs can add up flow counters per BGP community and use the result for traffic analysis and engineering. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted or updated.

today: RFC 8549 is a Proposed Standard on the IETF Standards Track, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Report BGP Communities
sections.content:
IP Flow Information Export (IPFIX, RFC 7011) tells network administrators how much traffic flows where, using Information Elements (IEs) listed in an IANA registry. Existing IEs describe flows by IP address, IP prefix, AS number and BGP next hop. In a Tier 1 or Tier 2 operator backbone, IP address or prefix can be too fine-grained, while AS number can be too coarse.

A BGP community is a BGP path attribute. Operators plan community values to stand for groups of customers, services, or geographical and topological regions. If flow records carried the communities, traffic could be counted per customer type or per region. The registry had no IEs for that, which is the gap this RFC fills.

The RFC defines no new BGP community attributes. It also does not update the IPFIX specification (RFC 7011) or information model (RFC 7012); the IANA registry stays the complete reference for IEs.
sections.plainLanguage: Counting traffic by exact house address is too detailed, and counting by whole country is too vague. Operators already put stickers on routes to say things like 'mobile customers' or 'this region', so the report should include the sticker.

sections.title: Who Attaches the Community Information
sections.content:
The community of a flow could be worked out in three places. An IPFIX Mediator (RFC 6183) could correlate flows with BGP routes, but then it must learn BGP routes and do routing table lookups, which is not trivial. A Collector could run BGP or the BGP Monitoring Protocol (RFC 7854) and do the same lookups, with the added problem that the routing table may have changed by the time the flow data arrives.

The third place is the Exporter itself, usually a router. To fill in IEs such as bgpSourceAsNumber or bgpNextHopIPv4Address, the Exporter already holds the current BGP routing table and does the lookup. It can read the communities in the same step, so the extra load is minimal and the match is more accurate. The RFC therefore says the community information is RECOMMENDED to be exported directly by the Exporter using IPFIX.

The RFC also says this is not meant to replace BMP, which has its own use cases, and that it is not the only way to get community data for a flow. The new IEs apply to both IPv4 and IPv6 traffic, and both Exporters and Mediators can use them.
sections.plainLanguage: The router already looks up the route to decide where each packet goes, and the sticker is written right on that route. It is easiest if the router just writes down the sticker at that moment instead of making someone else look it up later.

sections.title: A Traffic Engineering Use Case
sections.content:
The RFC's example has transit network AS C between AS A and AS B. Routes from AS A carry communities A:X and A:Y for different geographic regions. Routes from AS B carry B:M for mobile customers and B:N for fixed line customers. By default traffic from A to B uses path C1-C2-C3 (Path-1). When the link between C1 and C2 is congested, moving all of it to path C1-C4-C3 (Path-2) would just congest Path-2.

With IPFIX reporting communities, the PCE or SDN controller in AS C can see traffic per community, or per community pair when both source and destination matter. It can then move only part of the load, for example the traffic from A:X by a route policy at Router C1, or the traffic from A:Y to B:M, from Path-1 to Path-2.
sections.plainLanguage: When one road is jammed, sending every car to the side road would jam that too. If you know which cars come from which neighborhood, you can send just one neighborhood's cars the other way.

sections.title: The Nine New Information Elements
sections.content:
There is one group of three IEs for each BGP community type. Each group has a single-community IE and two list IEs. The lists are basicList structures (RFC 6313), one for the communities matching a flow's source IP address and one for its destination IP address.

  • Standard (RFC 1997, a 32-bit value): bgpCommunity, bgpSourceCommunityList, bgpDestinationCommunityList.
  • Extended (RFC 4360, an 8-octet quantity): bgpExtendedCommunity, bgpSourceExtendedCommunityList, bgpDestinationExtendedCommunityList.
  • Large (RFC 8092, a 12-octet quantity suited to 4-octet ASNs): bgpLargeCommunity, bgpSourceLargeCommunityList, bgpDestinationLargeCommunityList.

The registry text says bgpExtendedCommunity MUST be 8 octets and bgpLargeCommunity MUST be 12 octets. Each list holds zero or more of the matching community IE.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three kinds of stickers: small, medium and large. For each kind there is a way to list the stickers for the sender and a separate list for the receiver.

sections.title: Message Size and Exporter Behavior
sections.content:
An IPFIX message can be at most 65535 bytes (RFC 7011), and a normal BGP message at most 4096 bytes (RFC 4271). Communities are path attributes in BGP Update messages, so all of them together cannot exceed 4096 bytes, and one IPFIX message has room for all communities of a flow's source and destination.

If BGP Update messages are extended to 65535 bytes, as in the Extended Message work the RFC cites, the communities for one flow could in theory overflow an IPFIX message. The RFC notes that real routes usually carry no more than ten communities. BGP speakers that support the extended message SHOULD only convey as many communities as fit in the 65535-byte IPFIX limit. A Collector that receives a maximum-length message SHOULD log a warning that communities may be truncated, and the export policy should then be configured to limit communities. The RFC also notes that the IPFIX message length could be extended from 16 to 32 bits, but leaves the details out of scope.

A Collector SHOULD ignore a bgpExtendedCommunity or bgpLargeCommunity IE that is not the expected size, which protects BGP parsing code from invalid lengths. When an Exporter is asked by a template to report communities, it SHOULD do a BGP lookup using the flow's source or destination address and SHOULD include the communities in the message.
sections.plainLanguage: The envelope that carries the report has a size limit. A route's sticker list is always small enough to fit, except in a rare future case, where the receiver should say so if it looks cut off.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The same security considerations as for IPFIX (RFC 7011) and its information model (RFC 7012) apply. Those documents cover protecting stored data, restricting who can see it, confidentiality and integrity in transit, and authentication of Exporting and Collecting Processes.

The new point is trust. Communities can be used as an attack vector, so systems that act on community data from IPFIX must not assume it is credible and accurate. The RFC RECOMMENDS using only data the processing system can trust, for example communities generated by consecutive neighboring ASes in the same trust domain, meaning operated by the same carrier. It says no additional privacy risks are introduced.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone can put any sticker on a route, so do not trust a sticker unless it came from someone you know and trust.

sections.title: IANA Assignments and Encoding Example
sections.content:
IANA assigned nine ElementIDs, 483 to 491, in the IPFIX Information Elements registry. The single-community IEs are unsigned32 (standard) or octetArray (extended and large); the lists are basicList.

Appendix A shows an encoding. A template with ID 256 has four fields: source IPv4 address, destination IPv4 address, bgpSourceCommunityList (484) and bgpDestinationCommunityList (485). The list fields have field length 0xFFFF, meaning variable length, with the real length given by the basicList List Length. The example flow from 1.1.1.1 to 2.2.2.2 carries source communities 1:1001, 1:1002, 8:1001 and destination communities 2:1002, 8:1001. Each list starts with the semantic allof and refers to bgpCommunity (483) with field length 4.
sections.plainLanguage: Each new field got its own number in a big public list, so everyone's equipment uses the same number for the same thing. The example shows how a sender writes the numbers and stickers into one message.

items.desc: basicList of standard communities for the flow's source address.

items.label: bgpDestinationCommunityList
items.desc: basicList of standard communities for the flow's destination address.

items.label: bgpExtendedCommunity
items.desc: One BGP Extended Community; MUST be 8 octets.

items.label: bgpSourceExtendedCommunityList
items.desc: basicList of extended communities for the source address.

items.label: bgpDestinationExtendedCommunityList
items.desc: basicList of extended communities for the destination address.

items.label: bgpLargeCommunity
items.desc: One BGP Large Community; MUST be 12 octets.

items.label: bgpSourceLargeCommunityList
items.desc: basicList of large communities for the source address.

items.label: bgpDestinationLargeCommunityList
items.desc: basicList of large communities for the destination address.
